name: French

ancestors.notes: Frankish superstrate: /h/ restoration, initial stress, massive vocabulary (guerre, jardin, blanc). Strongest in Romance.
Gaulish substrate (already in la-x-gallia, additional direct traces)

notes:
Standard Metropolitan French (Parisian). Nasal grapheme sequences (⟨an⟩, ⟨am⟩, ⟨en⟩, ⟨em⟩, ⟨in⟩, ⟨im⟩, ⟨on⟩, ⟨om⟩, ⟨un⟩, ⟨um⟩) denasalise before a following vowel within the word (positional_graphemes before_vowel branch, e.g. amateur [amatœʁ], inutile [inytil], bonasse [bɔnas]); the ⟨n⟩/⟨m⟩-doubling trigger for denasalisation (immense, ennemi) is not separately modelled because the doubled consonant is tokenised as its own bb/dd/ff/gg/ll/mm/nn/pp/rr/tt digraph rather than surfacing as BEFORE_VOWEL/BEFORE_CONSONANT context on the nasal grapheme — a known engine-limit gap. Word-final unstressed ⟨e⟩ (e caduc) defaults to silent (positional_graphemes word_final), matching modern colloquial elision of the mute e; monosyllabic function words whose sole vowel is that final ⟨e⟩ (le, de, que, ce, ne, se, je, me, te) are handled via the word_exceptions whole-word override, since the positional-grapheme priority order always resolves WORD_FINAL before NUCLEUS_STRESSED and cannot express 'sole vowel nucleus of a monosyllable' as a rule — the schwa is grammatically obligatory there to preserve the syllable. FINAL CONSONANTS: t, d, p, s, x, r typically silent word-finally in modern French, resurfacing in liaison. LIAISON: s/x→[z], d/t→[t], n→[n] before vowel-initial words (sandhi_rules, obligatory after determiners/pronouns, optional after adjectives/prepositions per Tranel 1995). Aspirate-h words (les héros, le hibou) block both liaison and elision (Tranel 1995); this cannot currently be distinguished from mute-h words at the grapheme/sandhi level since ⟨h⟩ maps to the empty string in both cases — a lexical h-aspiré wordlist would be required, out of scope for this pass. Elision (le/la/je/de/que + vowel → l'/j'/d'/qu') is already resolved in standard orthography (words are written with the apostrophe), so it needs no additional G2P rule. SOFTENING: c→[s] before e/i/y; g→[ʒ] before e/i/y. INTERVOCALIC s: [z] between vowels within a word. Doubled consonants (bb, dd, ff, gg, ll, mm, nn, pp, rr, tt) degeminate to a single consonant, the modern-French default (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987). Modern Parisian speech increasingly merges /œ̃/ into /ɛ̃/ (brun/brin, un/hein); both realizations are kept as allophones of œ̃ rather than collapsing the phonemic contrast, since conservative Standard French sources (Fougeron & Smith 1993) still treat them as distinct. GLIDE FORMATION: word-internal ⟨i⟩ before another vowel letter glides to [j] (pied [pje], lion [ljɔ̃], fiacre [fjakʁ]) — positional_graphemes before_vowel branch, Tranel (1987) §5-6 on high-vowel gliding; the plain vowel-letter ⟨i⟩ (unlike the ⟨y⟩/⟨ien⟩/⟨oui⟩ digraphs already carrying [j]) previously always surfaced as the full vowel. This is blocked (BEFORE_FINAL_VOWEL, an engine-level position, see orthography2ipa/types.py) when the following vowel is itself the word's last audible slot — word-final unmarked ⟨ie⟩ stays [i], not [j+deleted-e]: vie [vi], envie [ɑ̃vi], folie [fɔli], Algérie [alʒeʁi], and the plural vies [vi] (⟨s⟩ is a transparent, independently-silenced suffix grapheme, Tranel 1987 §3) — without this exclusion the glide rule wrongly produces a vowel-less [vj] for the entire closed class of French nouns ending in unstressed ⟨-ie⟩/⟨-ies⟩. ILL EXCEPTION CLASS: ⟨ill⟩ is [ij] by default (fille, famille, bastille) except in a closed irregular set where it stays [il] — ville, mille, tranquille (and tranquillement) and the place name Lille — handled via word_exceptions per Tranel (1987) §4.3's irregular-ill list, since the digraph mapping cannot express a lexical exception to its own default. Sources: Fouché (1959), Tranel (1987), Ladefoged & Maddieson (1996), Fougeron & Smith (1993), Tranel (1995). word_exceptions also carry Tranel 1987 §7's closed list of common words whose final ⟨s⟩ is exceptionally pronounced (fils [fis], os, ours, mars, maïs, tennis, sens...); regular final ⟨s⟩ stays silent, and ambiguous homographs (tous, plus) are deliberately excluded. MUTE ⟨-er⟩/⟨-ez⟩ ENDINGS: deliberately NOT modelled as grapheme keys. ENDING "er" is [e] — the infinitive, the -er/-ier adjective and the agent noun lose the final consonant of the grammatical ending (parler, manger, boulanger, and boulangers behind the transparent plural) (Fouché 1959, Traité de prononciation française; Tranel 1987 §3 on final-consonant elision in grammatical endings). ENDING "ez" is [e] — the 2pl inflection and the frozen nez/chez/assez, the same elision in the same environment (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §3). Word-final ⟨-er⟩/[e] (parler) vs /ɛʁ/ (mer, hiver, super, loanwords) and ⟨-ez⟩/[e] (mangez, nez) are a MORPHOLOGICAL split — the mute reading belongs to the infinitive/2pl/agent-noun endings, not to the letter sequence — and morpheme chunks are forbidden grapheme keys (an ⟨er⟩ digraph makes ⟨s⟩ in pers-/vers- look intervocalic → *[pɛʁzɔn], and out-munches ⟨rr⟩ degemination → *[tɛʁʁ]); needs a morpheme-aware engine context (same follow-up as English suffix palatalization). The general word-final ⟨r⟩ silencing above covers the mute class at the letter level; the words whose final ⟨r⟩ IS pronounced (the mer/fer/hiver monosyllable-and-friends set plus English -er loanwords keeping /œʁ/~/ɛʁ/) are lexical exceptions carried in word_exceptions. FINAL ⟨r⟩ IS PRONOUNCED: the earlier word_final [""] made silence the DEFAULT for every final ⟨r⟩, which is the inverse of the fact — French word-final ⟨r⟩ is [ʁ] (mer, bonjour, sur, par, hiver, amour, chanteur); it is mute only in the ⟨-er⟩ sequence (infinitives parler, -er/-ier nouns and adjectives boulanger, premier), and that case is already owned by the grammatical_endings ⟨er⟩→[e] rewrite, which runs after the beam and also absorbs the transparent plural ⟨-ers⟩ (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §3). word_final is therefore ["ʁ", ""] — pronounced first, silence kept as the second beam branch for the monosyllabic-lexical residue. VERBAL ⟨-ent⟩ IS AMBIGUOUS AND IS EXPOSED, NOT DECIDED: the 3rd-person-plural inflection ⟨-ent⟩ is silent (ils parlent [paʁl], munissent [mynis]) while the nominal/adjectival ⟨-ent⟩ is [ɑ̃] (vent, dent, cent, argent, accent, talent, absent, serpent, Occident, Vincent). Verb-vs-noun is not decidable from spelling; it needs part-of-speech, which this layer does not have and (owner ruling) does not accept as an input — that decision belongs to a downstream rescorer. A rewriting ⟨ent⟩→[] entry is still NOT shipped: it wins 3844 wikipron/fr types against 254 losses, but the 254 are far commoner in running text than the inflected verb forms it wins, and this library feeds TTS; the counter-set is also open (Laurent, Florent, Clément), so it cannot go in word_exceptions. (NOTE, two different measurements, do not conflate them: 3844/254 is the ENGINE OUTCOME of the rewrite — types whose 1-best would move toward or away from gold if the rewrite shipped, so it depends on what the rest of the spec already gets right; 3873/287 below is a property of the GOLD ALONE — ⟨-ent⟩ types whose reference transcription is mute versus nasal, counted by string operations with no engine run. The two are close because the spec is mostly right on this class, not because they measure the same thing.) What IS shipped is the deferring candidate list "ent": [null, ""]. ENDING "ent" is [ɑ̃] or mute — both readings are attested for the same spelling, the mute one being the 3PL inflection and the nasal one the noun or adjective (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §3; Divay & Vitale 1997, which uses this very ending as the standard worked example of a grapheme-to-phoneme rule that requires part of speech). Element 0 is null, so rank 1 stays exactly what nasal ⟨en⟩ + silent ⟨t⟩ already produced (every 1-best byte-identical, vent [vɑ̃], moment [mɔmɑ̃], comment [kɔmɑ̃] unchanged), and the mute reading is added below rank 1 — measured at rank 4 for parlent, munissent and vent, rank 5 for moment, dorment and argent, i.e. below the ⟨e⟩ and final-⟨t⟩ branches the beam already carried. LATTICE-HOLE EVIDENCE for "ent" (the admissibility bar in SCHEMA.md, 0-in-top-k on gold): on a 300-word random sample of the gold-mute ⟨-ent⟩ class from wikipron/fr (fra_latn_broad), the gold mute reading appeared in word_candidates 0 times out of 300 anywhere in the top 10 before this entry, and 192 times out of 300 after it; exact@1 is 0 before and 0 after, because o2i does not decide. [paʁl] was in no beam at any width, so no downstream rescorer could ever recover it — a coverage hole, not a ranking error. ORDERING BASIS for "ent": rank 1 defers to the base path, i.e. to [ɑ̃], the majority reading in running text — the nominal/adjectival class (vent, dent, cent, argent) is far commoner in text than the inflected verb forms, even though gold TYPES run 3873 mute against 287 nasal, and this library feeds TTS, where type counts do not price a mispronounced vent. The mute alternative is gold-attested for the 3PL class and cited (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §3; Divay & Vitale 1997). LOI DE POSITION for ⟨eu⟩: [ø] in an open syllable (heureux, peu, jeu), [œ] in a closed one (fleur, chanteur, jeune) — Fougeron & Smith (1993), loi de position; Tranel (1987) ch. 4. Expressed with the OPEN_SYLLABLE/CLOSED_SYLLABLE positions. HOW APERTURE IS DECIDED, and what that costs: the law is about a PRONOUNCED coda, but the engine has only letters, so open/closed is an ORTHOGRAPHIC proxy — strip the graphemes this spec declares silent word-finally, then ask what the syllable ends in. On top of that, a final syllable with no audible nucleus (a mute ⟨e⟩: jeu·ne, eu·re) is folded into the syllable before it, whose coda its consonants really are (positional.merge_nucleusless_final_syllable, generic and spec-driven), and the strip then runs a SECOND time on that merged string — on letters that are no longer word-final in the pronunciation. So meute [møt] and heureuse [øʁøz] come out right for the wrong reason (both strip back to an open meu/reu although /t/ and /z/ are pronounced), and the proxy is outright wrong for a pronounced coda that does not close for the law (obstruent + liquid: neutre [nøtʁ] and feutre [føtʁ] get [œ]) and for a /z/ spelled ⟨z⟩, which cannot be stripped and is instead handled by FR_EU_BEFORE_Z. The same law is NOT declared for ⟨o⟩ or ⟨e⟩, and the proxy is why. ⟨o⟩: generalising close [o] to every open syllable is the SOUTHERN pattern (Walker 2001 ch. 3); standard French keeps [ɔ] in non-final open syllables (homophone [ɔmɔfɔn], obole [ɔbɔl], homme [ɔm]), and the aperture rule measured PER 0.0887 → 0.1177 on wikipron/fr, 16836 types worse against 447 better — so ⟨o⟩ stays on FR_O_FINAL_OPEN plus FR_O_BEFORE_Z. ⟨e⟩: French ⟨e⟩ is [ɛ] in a GRAPHICALLY closed syllable whether or not the coda is pronounced (met [mɛ], mets [mɛ], effets [efɛ]), which is the opposite of what a phonetic-coda proxy answers, so it keeps the orthographic FR_E_CLOSED_CLUSTER / FR_E_CLOSED_FINAL rules; the aperture version measured 0.0887 → 0.0903. 2026-08 LOANWORD -ER SNAPSHOT EXTENSION: the English-loan -er/[œʁ]~[ɛʁ] carve-out above (leader, cracker, container, poker, revolver) is a documented instance of an OPEN class, not a closed one — French keeps borrowing English agent-noun -er coinages on an ongoing basis, and proper nouns (surnames, place names) ending -er with gold /ʁ/ are unboundedly open by definition. A full closed-set fix via word_exceptions is therefore not possible without violating the closed-lexical-class rule (AGENTS.md §2). What IS shipped: 56 additional word_exceptions entries — every wikipron fr gold type ending ⟨-er⟩ with a SINGLE, unambiguous gold /ʁ/-final transcription (disagreement across wikipron entries for the same word, e.g. quaker, hamburger, manager, master, panzer, was treated as evidence of genuine synchronic variation and those words were deliberately left OUT rather than picking a transcription arbitrarily). A further 47 candidate types were audited against gold and dropped for a distinct, more specific reason than plain variation: their gold has BOTH an [e]-final and an [œʁ]/[ɛʁ]-final transcription, and the two readings are not free variation of the same word but a VERB–NOUN HOMOGRAPH split — mute-⟨er⟩ infinitive (and 2pl/agent-noun) morphology already covered by the grammatical_endings ⟨er⟩→[e] rewrite above versus the loanword agentive -er nominal reading this carve-out targets. Some are native French verbs (porter, reporter, poster, cacher, ranger, fier); most are English loan STEMS that French freely verbs with its own -er infinitive morphology the moment they are borrowed — denominal-verb formation from an English -er noun/agent borrowing (dealer/"to deal drugs", hacker/"to hack", zapper, spammer, streamer, scanner, mixer…) — so the SAME orthographic type is simultaneously a noun keeping /œʁʕ/ɛʁ/ ("un dealer") and a verb infinitive taking [e] ("dealer de la drogue"). A context-free lexical override in word_exceptions cannot express that split: it would silently mispronounce every verbal use of these types. This is a real ceiling of the whole-word-override layer, not an oversight — verb-vs-noun for this class needs part-of-speech, the same gap already documented above for the VERBAL ⟨-ent⟩ class, and is left to a morphology-aware pass / the ambiguity lattice and downstream rescorers rather than resolved by guessing one reading here. The 47 excluded types (with both gold readings) are: biker, bomber, boxer, cacher, carter, clipper, cruiser, dealer, designer, destroyer, driver, ester, fier, flipper, flyer, follower, gaffer, hacker, hamster, kicker, loader, loser, mixer, outsider, pointer, porter, poster, pranker, putter, quinter, ranger, rapper, recorder, reporter, scanner, skipper, spammer, spoiler, sprinter, starter, streamer, supporter, taler, trader, tuner, tweeter, zipper. Proper nouns (Jupiter, Esther, Jennifer, Khmer, Vancouver, Christopher, Miller, Niger, Roger...) were also deliberately left OUT of this pass — the onomastic class is open by construction and no finite word_exceptions list will ever be complete for it; they remain a documented, not a silently missed, gap. This is an ATTESTED-IN-THIS-GOLD-SNAPSHOT extension of the existing carve-out, not a claim of exhaustive coverage: new unambiguous English -er loans and new proper nouns will keep needing individual word_exceptions additions as they are attested in future gold, and the 47 homograph types remain a known gap for whichever future layer gets part-of-speech.

BARE ⟨-ent⟩ 3PL — DOWNSTREAM-RESCORER CEILING. Bare ⟨-ent⟩ stays list-valued (null or empty) because it spells both the mute 3PL verbal inflection and the nasal ending of a noun, adjective or adverb, and only part of speech separates them (Divay & Vitale 1997). A prior draft of this wave tried to carve out the longer 3PL desinences (⟨-aient -èrent -assent -issent -irent -urent⟩) as single-valued endings on the theory that their extra tense/mood morphology made them verb-only. That was wrong on two counts: Laurent (proper noun, gold [lɔʁɑ̃]) ends in the same letters as ⟨-urent⟩'s tail and is not a verb form, and — more seriously — each ending was a plain-string tail rewrite with no stem condition, so it clobbered the stem vowel of any OTHER verb whose 3PL happens to share the letters (courent misread as cour+ent, meurent, paraissent, croissent, puissent). Both failures are inherent to enumerating paradigm cells as context-free string endings rather than modelling the verbal stem; they are dropped and not reintroduced in any form. Reaching them correctly needs the same POS layer bare ⟨-ent⟩ is already waiting on (Divay & Vitale 1997).

NASAL VOWEL BLOCKING. A vowel letter plus ⟨n⟩ or ⟨m⟩ spells a nasal vowel only when the nasal letter closes the syllable — that is, only when it is neither doubled nor followed by a vowel letter. When either of those holds, the nasal consonant is a syllable ONSET, it is pronounced, and the vowel in front of it stays oral: ⟨-aine⟩ [ɛn] (Africaine [afʁikɛn]), ⟨-ienne⟩ [jɛn] (Adrienne [adʁjɛn]), ⟨aim-⟩ before a vowel [ɛm] (aimer [ɛme]), against the nasal readings of ⟨-ain⟩, ⟨-ien⟩ and ⟨-aim⟩ when a consonant or the word edge follows (bien [bjɛ̃], ancien [ɑ̃sjɛ̃]) (Tranel 1987 §3 on nasal vowels and their orthographic conditioning; Walker 2001; Fouché 1959). The spec's ⟨an/am/en/em/in/im/on/om/un/um⟩ sequences already get this from the coda condition on FR_NASAL_*; the multigraph spellings ⟨ain aim ein ien oin⟩ carry their nasal in the grapheme itself and need the same condition stated over them, which is what the FR_NASAL_BLOCK_* rules do.

YOD FROM ⟨il⟩ AFTER A VOWEL LETTER. Latin geminate -LL- palatalised to the "l mouillé", which in modern French has merged with the glide [j]. After a VOWEL letter, ⟨il⟩ and ⟨ill⟩ therefore spell [j] alone, not [l] or [ij]: travail [tʁavaj], soleil [sɔlɛj], bouteille [butɛj], feuille [fœj], ailleurs [ajœʁ] (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §5 on the glides; Walker 2001). The doubled spellings ⟨aill eill euill ouill ueill⟩ have this value in every position; the single ⟨ail eil euil ouil ueil⟩ have it only when the syllable is closed by the ⟨l⟩ — before a vowel letter the ⟨l⟩ is an ordinary onset and the preceding digraph keeps its own value (aile [ɛl] against ail [aj]). After a CONSONANT letter ⟨ill⟩ keeps the older [ij] (fille [fij], famille [famij]), which the existing context-free ⟨ill⟩ entry already supplies.

ASSIBILATION OF ⟨ti⟩ IN LEARNED WORDS. In the Latinate suffixes borrowed into French, ⟨t⟩ before ⟨i⟩ plus a vowel assibilated to [s]. These are ``grammatical_endings`` (word-final-bound), not ``graphemes`` (context-free), because unlike bare ⟨ti⟩ they are morpheme-final chunks that must not fire word-internally (⟨-tionn-⟩ of national, ⟨-tional⟩ of dictionnaire) — precedent: en-GB.json's own ⟨tion stion tial stial⟩ entries. ENDING "tion" is [sjɔ̃] (nation) (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §3). ENDING "stion" is [stjɔ̃] (question, gestion, bastion) — the change did not apply after ⟨s⟩, where the cluster kept its stop (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §3). ENDING "tial" is [sjal] (initial) (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §3). ENDING "tiel" is [sjɛl] (partiel) (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §3). ENDING "tience" is [sjɑ̃s] (patience) (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §3). The assibilation is a property of these suffixes, not of ⟨ti⟩ generally — ordinary ⟨ti⟩ before a vowel stays [tj] (pitié [pitje], moitié) — so it is stated as those suffix spellings and no wider.

DOUBLE CONSONANT LETTERS AND ⟨sc⟩/⟨cc⟩. French has no phonetic geminates: a doubled consonant letter spells a single consonant (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §2). The spec already carried ⟨bb dd ff gg ll mm nn pp rr tt ss⟩; ⟨ck⟩, ⟨kk⟩ and ⟨cqu⟩ are the same single [k] in a different spelling (Annick [anik], Becquart [bəkaʁ]). ⟨cc⟩ and ⟨sc⟩ are the two spellings where the second letter is a ⟨c⟩ that still softens: before a front vowel they are [ks] and [s] (accent [aksɑ̃], Ascension [asɑ̃sjɔ̃]), elsewhere the plain [k] and [sk] (accord [akɔʁ], scandale [skɑ̃dal]) (Fouché 1959).

HONEST RESIDUAL — bare verbal ⟨-ent⟩. The 3PL ⟨-ent⟩ of verbs whose stem does not end in one of the desinences listed above (abattent, abdiquent, abandonnent) stays ambiguous here on purpose: separating it from nominal ⟨-ent⟩ needs part of speech, which this engine does not have (Divay & Vitale 1997). It is a real and measurable residual, not a modelling ceiling.

HONEST RESIDUAL — ⟨-tions⟩ and the other POS collisions. The suffix-bound ⟨ti⟩ assibilation above is stated over spellings, and two French forms share a spelling with those suffixes: the 1PL imperfect/subjunctive in ⟨-tions⟩ of a stem ending in ⟨t⟩ (nous aboutions [abutjɔ̃], nous adaptions [adaptjɔ̃]) is spelled exactly like the plural of a ⟨-tion⟩ noun (nations [nasjɔ̃]), and ⟨-tial⟩ appears in bestial [bɛstjal] with the same ⟨st⟩ context the ⟨-stion⟩ entry covers only for ⟨-tion⟩. Measured against the full fr wikipron gold, this wave improves 9436 words and worsens 155, of which 72 are ⟨-tions⟩ verb forms. Separating them needs part of speech, which this engine does not have (Divay & Vitale 1997), so they are left wrong rather than pinned word by word.

FINAL-CONSONANT DELETION SEES THROUGH THE TRANSPARENT PLURAL. The word-final consonant a root loses (⟨petit⟩ [pəti], ⟨mot⟩ [mo], ⟨nid⟩ [ni], ⟨drap⟩ [dʁa]) is still lost when the plural or 2SG ⟨-s⟩/⟨-x⟩ is written behind it, because that suffix is itself silent and leaves the root-final letter as the word's last audible slot: ⟨petits⟩ [pəti], ⟨mots⟩ [mo], ⟨nids⟩ [ni], ⟨draps⟩ [dʁa], ⟨temps⟩ [tɑ̃] (Tranel 1987 §3 on final-consonant elision and on ⟨-s⟩/⟨-x⟩ as a transparent grammatical marker; Fouché 1959). The engine already carried that transparency for a VOWEL in the last audible slot (the ⟨vie⟩/⟨vies⟩ case), but not for a consonant, so ⟨mots⟩ came out *[mɔt] with the ⟨t⟩ audible and the syllable wrongly closed. The promotion reaches exactly one slot, so a letter further back is untouched and keeps whatever it has: ⟨corps⟩ is [kɔʁ], with ⟨p⟩ silent and ⟨r⟩ pronounced, and ⟨toujours⟩ stays [tuʒuʁ]. The promotion is floored at the word's first slot: with nothing audible in front of it there is no root for the suffix to be transparent TO, and silencing it would delete the word's only segment — ⟨DS⟩, ⟨ts⟩, ⟨ps⟩ would transcribe as the empty string. RESIDUAL: 44 wikipron fr types whose final cluster IS pronounced now lose it. They are three different strata, not one: initialisms read letter by letter (⟨BZDs⟩, ⟨IDS⟩, ⟨TPS⟩, ⟨VPS⟩); NATIVE Latinate adjectives and nouns whose learned final cluster is pronounced (⟨abjects⟩, ⟨abrupts⟩, ⟨exacts⟩, ⟨prompts⟩, ⟨incorrects⟩, ⟨relaps⟩, ⟨karsts⟩); and English/Latin loan plurals (⟨chips⟩, ⟨clips⟩, ⟨biceps⟩, ⟨forceps⟩, ⟨schnaps⟩, ⟨yaourts⟩). All three are open classes — new initialisms and new borrowings keep arriving, and the learned-cluster adjectives are not separable from the regular ones by spelling — so they are left wrong rather than pinned word by word, exactly as the ⟨-er⟩ loanword class above.

THE CIRCUMFLEX AND THE GRAVE DO NOT CHANGE A VOWEL DIGRAPH'S VALUE. The circumflex on a French vowel digraph is etymological — it marks an ⟨s⟩ the word lost (⟨coste⟩ > ⟨coût⟩, ⟨aoust⟩ > ⟨août⟩, ⟨jeusne⟩ > ⟨jeûne⟩, ⟨maistre⟩ > ⟨maître⟩) — and the digraph keeps the value it has unaccented (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 ch. 2). ⟨oû⟩ is ⟨ou⟩ [u] (goût, coûte, voûte, soûl, moût, ragoût); ⟨aî⟩ is ⟨ai⟩ [ɛ] (naît, faîtes, aînesse, maître); ⟨eû⟩ is ⟨eu⟩ [ø]~[œ] (jeûne, eût); ⟨oî⟩ is ⟨oi⟩ [wa] (cloître, croître). Without these keys the tokenizer split them into the plain letter plus the accented letter (⟨o⟩+⟨û⟩ → *[ɔy] for goût, ⟨a⟩+⟨î⟩ → *[ai] for naît), which is neither reading French has. ⟨où⟩ is the same digraph ⟨ou⟩ [u]; its grave is not a phonetic mark at all but the graphic device that keeps the relative/interrogative apart from the conjunction ⟨ou⟩ (Fouché 1959). The claim is about the DIGRAPHS: the single accented letters ⟨î ê â ù û⟩ are untouched and keep their existing values.

INTERVOCALIC ⟨y⟩ COUNTS AS TWO ⟨i⟩. Between two vowel letters, ⟨y⟩ does the work of a vowel-⟨i⟩ and a glide-⟨i⟩ at once: the first joins the preceding vowel letter into that letter's own digraph, the second surfaces as [j] — ⟨royal⟩ is ⟨roi⟩+⟨ial⟩ [ʁwajal], ⟨voyer⟩ [vwaje], ⟨croyons⟩ [kʁwajɔ̃], ⟨appuyer⟩ [apɥije], ⟨payer⟩ [pɛje], ⟨rayon⟩ [ʁɛjɔ̃], ⟨asseyez⟩ [asɛje] (Fouché 1959; Tranel 1987 §5 on the glides; Walker 2001). Stated as positional_graphemes on ⟨oy uy ay ey⟩ with a before_vowel branch, since with no following vowel letter there is no second ⟨i⟩ and only the digraph surfaces: ⟨Roy⟩ [ʁwa], ⟨Puy⟩ [pɥi], ⟨Épinay⟩ [epinɛ]. ⟨ay⟩ carries [ɛj] first and [aj] second, and ⟨ai⟩'s own [ɛ]/[e] alternation is inherited: the [aj] reading is real but minority (⟨mayonnaise⟩ [majɔnɛz], ⟨papaye⟩, ⟨cobaye⟩ against ⟨crayon⟩ [kʁɛjɔ̃], ⟨rayon⟩, ⟨ayez⟩ [ɛje]), so it is ranked, not chosen. RESIDUAL: 55 gold types where ⟨y⟩ after a vowel letter is [ɔj]/[aj] rather than the digraph — the IUPAC acyl nomenclature (benzoyle, alcoyle, halloysite), the ⟨ouïr⟩ forms (oyais, oyait), and onomastic/loan material (boy, arroyo, Haydn, Fayçal). Both strata are open classes; they are documented here rather than pinned. The ⟨pays⟩/⟨paysage⟩ family is a fourth, etymological case — its ⟨ay⟩ is [ei], the trace of an older ⟨païs⟩ hiatus — and the class RE-SHUFFLES rather than simply regressing: 42 types move, the inflected ⟨paysage-⟩ forms improve and the short ones do not, for a net gain of 0.27 PER-units. It is left as measured rather than lexicalised.

WORD-FINAL ⟨ai⟩ IS CLOSE-MID. ⟨ai⟩ with nothing after it is [e] — ⟨j'ai⟩ [ʒe], ⟨vrai⟩ [vʁe], ⟨quai⟩ [ke], ⟨balai⟩, ⟨essai⟩, and the 1SG futures ⟨chanterai⟩ — while ⟨ai⟩ followed by any consonant letter, pronounced or not, is [ɛ]: ⟨mais⟩ [mɛ], ⟨lait⟩ [lɛ], ⟨français⟩ [fʁɑ̃sɛ], ⟨parfait⟩, and the conditionals ⟨chanterais⟩/⟨chanterait⟩ (the loi de position stated for the word's last syllable, Walker 2001; Fouché 1959). Expressed as FR_AI_FINAL_CLOSE_MID, an allophone rule conditioned on followed_by word_boundary — the TRUE word edge, not the WORD_FINAL position, which the transparent ⟨-s⟩/⟨-x⟩ promotion above also reaches. Stated as a word_final positional entry instead, the same claim reads ⟨-ais⟩ as effectively final, turns every conditional into a future and gives ⟨mais⟩ *[me] and ⟨français⟩ *[fʁɑ̃se]; measured on the full wikipron fr gold that variant is 0.0707 against 0.0673 for the rule shipped here. THIS CLAIM IS GOLD-DEPENDENT AND THE TWO GOLD SETS DISAGREE DIAMETRICALLY, so it is recorded as a choice, not as a fact both sources confirm. In wikipron fr (Wiktionary, human-sourced) word-final ⟨ai⟩ is [e] in 1467 types against [ɛ] in 68; in ipadict fr (machine-generated, phonemizer-lineage) it is [ɛ] in 9236 types against [e] in 49. This spec follows wikipron and the reference grammars, on the reasoning that a human-transcribed source outranks a phonemizer's own output for a distinction that is precisely about orthoepic tradition (Walker 2001; Fouché 1959), and that the ipadict PER improves anyway (0.0785 → 0.0768) even though its exact match falls, because the disagreement is one segment deep. The [ɛ] reading is NOT in the beam at any k: FR_AI_FINAL_CLOSE_MID is an allophone rewrite (ɛ→e), which removes the [ɛ] candidate from the lattice rather than demoting it — the same coverage-hole shape documented above for the mute ⟨-ent⟩ reading before its list-valued entry. A downstream consumer targeting the phonemizer convention cannot recover [ɛ] by re-ranking; that would need a spec-level alternative, which is a known lattice hole of this rule. RESIDUAL within wikipron: 67 types whose final ⟨ai⟩ is [ɛ] there too (⟨mai⟩, ⟨lai⟩, ⟨geai⟩, ⟨Tournai⟩) — the 4.4% minority is left wrong rather than lexicalised.

REFUTED IN THIS WAVE — THE UNLIGATED ⟨oe⟩/⟨oeu⟩ SPELLINGS. Adding ⟨oeu⟩ [ø]~[œ] and ⟨oe⟩ [œ] as graphemes, so that the typewriter spellings of ⟨œu⟩/⟨œ⟩ transcribe like the ligature (⟨oeuf⟩, ⟨boeuf⟩, ⟨coeur⟩), measured 0.0674 against 0.0673 — no gain — and broke ⟨coefficient⟩ [kɔefisjɑ̃] → *[kœfisjɛ̃], ⟨moelle⟩ and ⟨Noel⟩, where ⟨oe⟩ is genuinely two vowels. ⟨oe⟩ is a typographic substitution for a character the writer could not type, not a French grapheme, so restoring the ligature is normalisation and belongs upstream of this library (AGENTS.md §7), not in the grapheme table.

sources.notes: Formalises liaison (silent word-final consonant surfaces before a vowel-initial word, e.g. les amis [lezami]) and elision (word-final vowel deleted before a vowel-initial word, e.g. l'ami) as ONSET-driven; establishes that h-aspiré words (hibou) block both liaison and elision despite being phonetically vowel-initial (les hiboux *[lezibu], le hibou *[libu]).

sources.author: Walker, D.C.
sources.title: French Sound Structure
sources.notes: States the loi de position and its limits for standard (Parisian/northern) French: close-mid /e ø o/ in open syllables against open-mid /ɛ œ ɔ/ in closed ones, with /ʁ/ an opening environment for the back vowel (⟨au⟩ + r), /z/ a closing-environment exception that keeps [o] (rose), and the alternation robust only in the word's last syllable — in non-final syllables the quality is largely lexical or harmonic (heureux [øʁø] beside fleurette [flœʁɛt]). Also documents the southern French pattern that generalises the law and which this spec deliberately does NOT model.

⟨e⟩ in a closed syllable is [ɛ], not schwa (Tranel 1987 §4: loi de position — Abel [abɛl], Albert [albɛʁ], mer, sel); e-caduc only occurs in open syllables. Two conditions cover closure: before a consonant cluster, and before a word-final consonant. A single letter spelling a consonant CLUSTER closes the syllable by itself (⟨x⟩ = /ks/: Alexandre [alɛksɑ̃dʁ]) — Tranel 1987 §4; Walker 2001.

⟨e⟩ in a closed syllable is [ɛ], not schwa (Tranel 1987 §4: loi de position — Abel [abɛl], Albert [albɛʁ], mer, sel); e-caduc only occurs in open syllables. Two conditions cover closure: before a consonant cluster, and before a word-final consonant.

⟨e⟩ in a closed syllable is [ɛ], not schwa (Tranel 1987 §4: loi de position — Abel [abɛl], Albert [albɛʁ], mer, sel); e-caduc only occurs in open syllables. Two conditions cover closure: before a consonant cluster, and before a word-final consonant.

Loi de position for /ɔ/ (Tranel 1987 §3): mid back vowel is close [o] in a word-final open syllable (mot [mo], numéro) and before /z/ (rose [ʁoz], chose); open [ɔ] in other closed syllables (bord, botte).

Loi de position for /ɔ/ (Tranel 1987 §3): mid back vowel is close [o] in a word-final open syllable (mot [mo], numéro) and before /z/ (rose [ʁoz], chose); open [ɔ] in other closed syllables (bord, botte).

⟨au⟩ is [ɔ], not its usual [o], before /ʁ/: Laure [lɔʁ], aurore [ɔʁɔʁ], restaurant [ʁɛstɔʁɑ̃], Aurélie [ɔʁeli], dinosaure [dinozɔʁ]. This is the one systematic exception to the otherwise exceptionless ⟨au⟩ = [o] of the loi de position, and it is stated as such by Fouché (1959), Traité de prononciation française, for ⟨au⟩ + r, by Tranel (1987), The Sounds of French, ch. 3, and by Walker (2001), French Sound Structure, ch. 3, all of which name /ʁ/ as an opening environment for the mid back vowel in standard (Parisian/northern) French. Modelled as Parisian, which is what the wikipron gold transcribes; a southern speaker generalises close [o] much more widely and would not want this rule. Residual counter-examples are learned or foreign (Saurat, nauruan, vaurien), where the spelling is not a native ⟨aur⟩ sequence.

⟨eu⟩ stays close-mid [ø] before /z/ even though the syllable is closed — Deleuze [dəløz], yeuz [jøz] — the front-rounded counterpart of the ⟨o⟩ rule FR_O_BEFORE_Z above (rose [ʁoz], chose). /z/ is the standard closing-environment exception to the loi de position, named as such by Fouché (1959), Traité de prononciation française, by Tranel (1987), The Sounds of French, §3, and by Walker (2001), French Sound Structure, ch. 3, which lists it for the whole mid series and not for the back vowel alone. Most French ⟨euse⟩ words (heureuse, creuse, chanteuse) already reach [ø] without this rule, because their mute ⟨e⟩ and mute-word-final ⟨s⟩ strip back to an open syllable; this rule covers the residue where the /z/ is spelled ⟨z⟩ and so is not strippable.

Word-final ⟨ai⟩ with nothing following is close-mid /e/ (⟨j'ai⟩ [ʒe], ⟨vrai⟩ [vʁe], ⟨quai⟩ [ke]), against open-mid /ɛ/ whenever a consonant letter follows it (⟨mais⟩ [mɛ], ⟨lait⟩ [lɛ]) — the loi de position stated for the last syllable of the word (Walker 2001; Fouché 1959).
